name: Grand Teton National Park
author: author-D-2026-10-08
summary:
With no foothills in the way, the jagged peaks and deep canyons of the Teton Range rise straight out of the valley of Jackson Hole. The rocks at the range’s core, 2.7 billion years old, are among the oldest in North America, yet the mountains are among the youngest in the world: for about 10 million years earthquakes on the Teton fault have lifted the range while the valley floor dropped, until the same rock layers lie nearly 30,000 feet apart. Glaciers up to 3,500 feet thick flowed down from Yellowstone and carved the skyline, leaving moraines that now dam lakes like Jenny Lake. The 310,000-acre park shelters some 1,200 kinds of plants, 300 of birds and more than 60 of mammals. [1]

People have used this valley for roughly 11,000 years, coming in the warm months to hunt and gather; homesteaders did not settle year-round until the mid-1880s. [2] [1] Protecting it took half a century of fighting. Congress created a 96,000-acre park around the peaks and lakes on February 26, 1929. John D. Rockefeller Jr., through the Snake River Land Company, bought more than 35,000 acres of the valley floor, and in 1943 President Franklin Roosevelt proclaimed Jackson Hole National Monument — over furious local opposition, including an armed cattle drive across the monument joined by the actor Wallace Beery. A compromise merged park and monument on September 14, 1950, after Rockefeller gave 32,117 acres to the nation; the HRS calls the result the culmination of 50 years of work, often marred by bitter controversy. [3]

indigenous.html:
Jackson Hole’s winters were too severe for year-round living, so for millennia its peoples came in season, following ripening plants and migrating game; the oldest buried cultural deposits in the park date to about 5,850 years ago. The mountain-dwelling people the first trappers met were Eastern Shoshone — the Tukudika, or Sheep-Eaters, who were still without horses when they were placed on the Wind River Reservation around 1868. The Shoshone still keep close ties here: in their belief system high peaks are “Power Mountain,” places to enter the spirit world through visions. [2]

Lt. Gustavus Doane, who led a near-disastrous winter expedition into Jackson Hole in 1876, is part of that history too. [4] In 2022 Yellowstone renamed Mount Doane as First Peoples Mountain; the Park Service’s announcement states that in 1870 Doane led an attack on a band of Piegan Blackfeet, the Marias Massacre, in which at least 173 people were killed, many of them women, elders and children sick with smallpox, and that he bragged of it for the rest of his life. [5] The Blackfeet are among the tribes Grand Teton lists as traditionally associated with the park. [6]

labor_ccc.html: When the Bureau of Reclamation dammed Jackson Lake, the rising water drowned the forest along its shores, and the dead and downed trees ringed the lake for years. Clearing them became the Civilian Conservation Corps’ biggest job in the valley. Young men aged 17 to 25 were stationed in camps at Leigh Lake, Lizard Point and near Colter Bay, and from 1934 at Camp NP-4 at the south end of Jenny Lake, manned through 1942. Between 1933 and 1937 they cleared the bulk of 7,000 acres of shoreline; by September 1936 crews were finishing the last 85 acres. They also built the Jenny Lake campground, trails to Phelps Lake and Garnet Canyon, telephone lines and staff housing, and several buildings from the Jenny Lake camp, meant to be temporary, remain in use today. [3]

sources.title: Daugherty, A Place Called Jackson Hole (HRS, 1999), ch. 17, Conservationists — Civilian Conservation Corps section

climate.html: The glaciers that carved the Tetons are now small remnants, and they are shrinking. The park’s 2017 foundation document reports that its glaciers and snowfields are getting smaller each year; records show both advance and retreat, but the overall trend is retreat, and models of Wyoming’s alpine glaciers under projected climate change predict the near-complete disappearance of Teton Glacier within 30 to 75 years. A 1968 USGS map showed 9 named glaciers and about 136 smaller glaciers or perennial snowfields, but the park has never completed a thorough inventory. The same document lists glacier retreat, thinner winter snowpack and lower lake levels among the effects of climate change on the park’s scenery, and expects more landslides and avalanches as climate variability brings more extreme events. [6] The brochure singles out whitebark pine, a keystone food source for grizzly bears and red squirrels, as sensitive to global climate change. [1]

facts.claim: No foothills; peaks rise abruptly from Jackson Hole valley; 2.7 billion-year-old core rocks among oldest in North America; mountains among youngest in the world
Teton fault movement beginning 10 million years ago; vertical displacement approaches 30,000 feet
Glaciers up to 3,500 feet thick flowed south from Yellowstone; moraines dam lakes like Jenny Lake; 310,000-acre park
1,200 plants, 300 birds, over 60 mammals, 12 fish
Native Americans did not live in the valley year-round because of severe winters; permanent residents from the mid-1880s
Slim Lawrence collection helped illuminate approximately 11,000 years of human habitation
Feb 26, 1929 Coolidge signed bill creating a 96,000-acre park including Teton Range and alpine lakes
Snake River Land Company acquired more than 35,000 acres (paid $1,400,310.04 for 35,310.396 acres)
1943 Roosevelt proclamation under Antiquities Act established Jackson Hole National Monument; transferred 130,000 acres from Teton National Forest
May 2, 1943 heavily armed ranchers trailed some 500 cattle across the monument; Wallace Beery's participation drew national attention

New Grand Teton NP created September 14, 1950 merging most of 1929 park and monument; Dec 16, 1949 Rockefeller conveyed 32,117 acres; 'culmination of 50 years work, often marred by bitter controversy'
Prehistoric people resided in the valley seasonally following ripening plants and game
Oldest buried cultural deposits in GRTE radiocarbon-dated to around 5,850 years ago
First mountain-dwelling peoples met by trappers known as Sheep-eaters; Tukudika, Eastern Shoshone, still without horses when placed on the Wind River Reservation around 1868
For modern Shoshone, peaks are 'puhadoya' ('Power Mountain'), access to spirit world through visions or dreams
1876 Lt. Gustavus Cheney Doane led a small party of soldiers into Jackson Hole; winter expedition; poor planning; lucky to survive

June 9, 2022: Mount Doane renamed First Peoples Mountain; 1870 Doane led an attack on a band of Piegan Blackfeet (Marias Massacre); at least 173 killed incl. many women, elderly and children suffering from smallpox; Doane wrote fondly about it and bragged for the rest of his life
Blackfeet Tribe of the Blackfeet Indian Reservation of Montana listed as traditionally associated tribe
Jackson Lake dam flooded shoreline trees; CCC enrollees 17–25; camps at Leigh Lake, Lizard Point, 'Hot Springs' near Colter Bay; Camp NP-4 at south end of Jenny Lake built 1934, manned through 1942
